introduction-the-chaos-of-v20-final-fina.core: Version numbers are a promise about compatibility. Without a shared scheme, consumers can't tell whether an upgrade is safe, and releases become guesswork.

first_principles.problem: A 'minor' update silently changes an API, and every downstream user's build breaks.
truths: Consumers decide whether to upgrade based on version numbers.
derivation: Write **Conventional Commits** so history is machine-readable.

analogy.title: A car part labelled 'fits 2019 models'
analogy.story: If the bolt pattern changed mid-year without a new label, the part wrecks engines.
analogy.breaks: Numbers only help if maintainers honour them.

example.title: v2.0-final-final-real
example.scenario: A naming mess, then the fix.

check.q: What should a version number communicate?
check.a: Whether an upgrade is compatible, adds features, or breaks things.

semantic-versioning-semver.core: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: bump MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for backward-compatible features and PATCH for backward-compatible fixes. 0.x means 'anything may change'.

first_principles.problem: Consumers need to know at a glance whether `^1.4.2` can safely auto-update.
truths: Changes are breaking, additive or fixes.
Dependency ranges rely on version meaning.

analogy.title: Building renovations
analogy.story: Repainting (patch), adding a room (minor) or knocking down a load-bearing wall (major), which everyone needs warning about.
analogy.breaks: The 'breaking' judgement can be subjective. Behaviour changes also count.

check.q: Removing a public function requires which bump?

conventional-commits.core: Commit messages follow `type(scope): description`, with `!` or a BREAKING CHANGE footer for breaking changes. Tools can then derive the next SemVer bump from history.

first_principles.problem: 'fix stuff' and 'updates' give no way to compute versions or write release notes automatically.
truths: Commit history is the record of change.
derivation: Others (docs, chore, refactor, ci) → no release.

analogy.title: Labelled shipping boxes
analogy.story: 'Fragile', 'Perishable' and 'Hazardous' labels let the warehouse robots route boxes automatically.
analogy.breaks: Labels only work if they're accurate. Mislabelling a breaking change ships a wrong version.

code.text:
fix(auth): handle expired refresh tokens
feat(api): add pagination to /users
feat(api)!: rename /users to /accounts

BREAKING CHANGE: /users endpoint removed

check.q: Which commit type triggers a MINOR bump?

changelog-automation.core: Tools like semantic-release, release-please and changesets read conventional commits to compute the version, write CHANGELOG.md, tag and publish, with no human bookkeeping.

first_principles.problem: Hand-written changelogs are forgotten, vague ('various fixes') and inconsistent.
truths: Structured commits already describe each change.

analogy.title: An accounting system that writes its own ledger
analogy.story: Every transaction is labelled, so the monthly statement assembles itself.
analogy.breaks: Generated notes are only as good as the commit messages, so you may still need a human summary.

example.title: release-please in GitHub Actions
flow: Merge PR → tag + GitHub release + publish

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Consistent releases with zero manual notes.

check.q: What does semantic-release need from the repository?
check.a: Commit messages in a parseable convention such as Conventional Commits.

enforcing-the-standard-with-commitlint.core: commitlint checks every commit message against the convention, both in a local commit-msg hook (husky) and in CI, because one malformed commit can break automated versioning.

first_principles.problem: A single 'WIP' commit in a release window produces the wrong version or none at all.
derivation: Also check **in CI** (hooks can be skipped).
Use **squash merges** with a validated PR title.

analogy.title: A form that rejects invalid entries
analogy.story: The web form won't submit until the date field is a real date.
analogy.breaks: Local hooks can be bypassed with --no-verify, so CI is the real gate.

example.title: Setting it up

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: `git commit -m "stuff"` is rejected with a helpful message.

code.text:
npm i -D @commitlint/cli @commitlint/config-conventional husky
echo "export default { extends: ['@commitlint/config-conventional'] }" > commitlint.config.js
npx husky add .husky/commit-msg 'npx --no -- commitlint --edit "$1"'

example.outcome: every commit fuels the release automation.

check.q: Why also run commitlint in CI if there's a local hook?
check.a: Hooks can be skipped or not installed, so CI guarantees enforcement.
